div.p: The flexible spin-lock model (FSLM) unifies suspension-based and spin-based resource access protocols for partitioned fixed-priority preemptive scheduling based real-time multi-core platforms. Recent work has been done in defining the protocol for FSLM, providing schedulability analysis, and investigating the practical consequences of the theoretical model.

FSLM complies to the AUTOSAR standard for the automotive industry, and prototype implementations of FSLM in the OSEK/VDX-complaint Erika Enterprise Real-Time Operating System have been realized. In this paper, we briefly describe some practical challenges to improve efficiency and generality.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In traditional lock-based resource access protocols (RAPs) for real-time multi-core platforms, a task that is blocked on a global resource either performs a non-preemptive busy wait, i.e. spins, or releases the core, i.e. suspends. The multiprocessor stack resource policy (MSRP) [11] is a spin-based protocol while the multi-processor priority ceiling protocol (MPCP) [13] is a suspension-based protocol. The flexible spinlock model (FSLM) [2] unifies both traditional approaches for partitioned fixed-priority preemptive scheduling (P-FPPS) by introducing a spin-lock priority for each processor, allowing the blocked task to spin at an arbitrary priority level. FSLM assumes FIFO-based resource queues and both non-nested as well non-preemptive global resource access. From a theoretical perspective, i.e. by excluding run-time overheads, FSLM significantly improves the schedulability ratio of systems compared to the spin-based and suspension-based approaches [3].

P-FPPS and spin-based global RAPs are also prescribed for multi-processor platforms by AUTOSAR [1], the standard for the automotive industry. Given the theoretical advantage of FSLM over the traditional RAPs and its compliance with AUTOSAR, initial investigations [5], [8] have been performed to determine how it performs from a practical perspective. FSLM has therefore been implemented in Erika Enterprise [10], a free of charge, open-source real-time operating system (RTOS), which was originally developed for small-scale OSEK/VDX [12] compatible embedded systems for the automotive market, and natively supports MSRP. The goals of these investigations were to determine (i) feasibility of implementation, (ii) induced overheads, (iii) extensibility of the analysis with dedicated terms for overheads, (iv) whether or not FSLM still outperforms MSRP when overheads are taken into account. Both investigations used an instantiation of the Erika Enterprise RTOS on Altera FPGA-based Nios II soft-core processors [9]. Whereas Erika Enterprise RTOS uses global low-level spin-lock variables for its native implementation of MSRP, both investigations used local lowlevel spin-lock variables and inter-core communication for the implementation of FSLM.

The results of a comparative evaluation of FSLM and MSRP indicated that FSLM becomes particularly attractive when the critical section length of tasks accessing global shared resources increases and the number of cores increases. The results also indicated that the overheads due to intercore communication are substantial. In particular, the Remote Notification (RN) mechanism provided by the Erika Enterprise RTOS, which uses shared data structures and an inter-core interrupt mechanism, gives rise to high overheads [5]. That mechanism was therefore replaced by a Dedicated Interrupt (DI) mechanism in [8], significantly reducing the inter-core communication overhead.

From these investigations, it was concluded that it is desirable to have a unified implementation of MSRP and FSLM in a single framework to reduce overheads and improve efficiency. Moreover, only a restricted range of spin-lock priorities of FSLM have been addressed by the initial investigations, providing options to improve generality. In the next section, we consider the resulting practical challenges for FSLM.

div.head: A. Unified implementation of MSRP and FSLM 1) Design:
div.p: The overhead of the natively provided MSRP implementation is considerably lower than FSLM. This is an immediate consequence of the fact that MSRP doesn't require inter-core communication, whereas both existing implementations of FSLM do. Both implementation of FSLM even require inter-core communication for instantiations of systems where the spin-lock priorities on all cores are the highest, i.e. conform MSRP. It is therefore desirable to have a unified implementation, in which inter-core communication is minimized, i.e. only used where necessary. To better understand where necessary, we first consider the existing implementations of MSRP and FSLM in some detail and subsequently revisit the challenge.

In MSRP, a task blocked on a resource always spins non-preemptively on a dedicated global low-level spin-lock variable. By allowing the blocked task to continuously poll that variable to check for the release of the resource, a releasing task can simply toggle that global variable. Hence, there is no need for a dedicated inter-core communication mechanism nor for a releasing task to know whether or not another task is waiting.

In FSLM, since it is possible for a spinning task that is blocked on a resource to be preempted by a higher priority task, simply toggling a global spin-lock variable upon resource release is no longer sufficient. Moreover, because a task releasing a resource needs to know which task, if any, shall be notified, a global field with mutual exclusive access is required. For FSLM, an additional local low-level spin-lock variable per core was used to reduce contention on shared data, together with an inter-core communication mechanism to allow a task releasing a resource to notify a remote core on which another task is blocked on the same resource.

In a unified implementation of MSRP and FSLM, notification by means of an inter-core communication mechanism is only required, if a task to be granted a global resource is executed on a core where the spin-lock priority is not the highest. In the special case where all tasks using a global resource are executed on cores where the spin-lock priority is highest, it may even be conceivable to revert to the MSRP implementation for that resource.
2) Analysis: In [8], the existing analyses for MSRP and FSLM were extended with dedicated terms for overheads. Whenever the implementation is unified, we may also unify the analysis.

div.head: B. Support for the entire spin-lock priority range
div.p: 1) Design: The implementations described in [5], [8] only provide support for a sub-range of spin-lock priorities. To be more specific, let a system consist of a set P of m identical cores P 0 , P 1 , . . ., P m-1 , let π max Pk represent the highest priority on core P k and let π G Pk denote the highest resource ceiling (or ceiling priority) of the global resources used on that core. Only spin-lock priorities from the range [π G Pk , π max Pk ] are supported by the implementations in [5], [8].

A main advantage of restricting the spin-lock priorities to this range is that at most one task on a core can have a pending global resource request, as proved by Lemma 12 in [2]. Accordingly, it is sufficient to just send an inter-core interrupt when a global resource is granted. Whenever the spin-lock priority range is extended, multiple tasks on a core may be blocked on different global resources. This gives rise to the following two challenges. Firstly, when the core receives a notification, the appropriate task needs to be identified. Secondly, when tasks on different remote cores release global resources simultaneously, it has to be guaranteed that all tasks that are granted resources on the same core actually become unblocked. The efficiency of the resulting implementation is clearly a challenge.

2) Analysis: For the time being, the analysis for FSLM has only be extended with dedicated terms for overhead for spin-lock priorities in the range [π G Pk , π max Pk ]. 3) Stack sharing: In the context of single-core systems, the stack resource policy (SRP) [6] allows tasks to share a single stack by preventing interleaved executions of tasks, thereby reducing memory requirements. MSRP, which generalizes SRP from a single core to a multi-core system, maintains this attractive property of allowing tasks that are executing on a single core to share a single stack. For a spin-lock priority π spin Pk of a core P k in the range [π G Pk , π max Pk ], it has been shown that FSLM allows the set of tasks on that core to require only two stacks, where tasks with a priority at most π spin Pk share one stack and the other tasks share a different stack; see [4], [7]. It is yet unclear, however, how many stacks are required for spin-lock priorities in the range [π min Pk , π G Pk ), where π min Pk represents the lowest priority on core P k .

III. CONCLUSION FSLM is a spin-based RAP for real-time multi-core systems based on P-FPPS, which complies with the AUTOSAR standard for the automotive domain. In earlier work, we demonstrated feasibility of FSLM in the OSEK/VDX-compliant Erika Enterprise RTOS, and determined induced overheads and extensibility of the analysis with dedicated terms for overheads. In this paper, we briefly presented some practical challenges for FSLM, in particular related to the efficiency and generality of the implementation and availability of the complementing analysis.
